title: Hausa cities: walls, markets and kings
intro: Walled towns grew across the Hausa lands of today's northern Nigeria. This chapter begins with Kano. Most of its early dates come from the Kano Chronicle, a history compiled from older traditions. It counts reigns by their length, so its years are a later reckoning and are labelled that way. The copy translated in 1908 was written down in the late nineteenth century; the historian Murray Last argues its first edition dates from the mid-1600s.

features.name: Kano · walled city
features.what: Kano grew around Dala hill. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning its first wall was begun between 1095 and 1134, and Muhammad Rumfa (1463–1499) built a palace, extended the walls through named gates and founded Kurmi market. The palace site, Gidan Rumfa, is still the emir's residence, and Kurmi still trades.
features.evidence: The Kano Chronicle (compiled from older traditions; Palmer's 1908 translation), Nigeria's 2007 heritage file, archaeology cited by Iliffe, and architectural history
features.location: Representative point for the old walled city, rounded; not a survey of the walls or gates.

monument.note: Original schematic stage set of an earth-built city, not a survey or reconstruction. Each part appears at its own date (listed under What appears when). The Chronicle names the gates but does not place them, so gate positions, wall lines, the palace footprint and the market are schematic; the walls are drawn as sun-dried earth (tubali) on a sloping profile with a crenellated crest. Nothing later is added: no present-day palace decoration (mostly 1930s–40s), no 1951 mosque or minaret, no 16th-century wall line, no emblem or bridge.

monument.note: Carries on from the previous scene's stage set as it stood in 1438; Rumfa's palace, walls and market rise again at their own date. People, camels and goods are small schematic figures with no faces, dress or likenesses, and their numbers are illustrative. The twenty-one towns of captives are shown as a count, because their places are not known. Roads are schematic.

features.name: Katsina
features.what: Another Hausa city, north-west of Kano. The Kano Chronicle records that Kano's first war with Katsina came in Rumfa's reign and lasted eleven years, with neither side winning.
features.location: Today's city centre, rounded. The fifteenth-century town's extent is not drawn.

features.name: Bornu
features.what: The kingdom east of Kano that grew from Kanem. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning, Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452) was the first Hausa king to send it tribute, and he opened the road from Bornu to Gwanja through Kano.
features.location: Drawn at Ngazargamu, which became Bornu's capital about 1472. The point stands for the kingdom, not a city.

scenes.title: The earth becomes a city

when.label: About 1000–1499 · archaeology and the Kano Chronicle

scenes.text: Before Kano was a city, it was a hill. People worked iron on Dala. The Kano Chronicle remembers Barbushe, keeper of a shrine on the hill. That memory is tradition, and it has no date. By the Chronicle's reckoning, King Gijimasu began a wall, gate by gate. Who finished it? The Chronicle says Yusa, in the 1100s. Nigeria's heritage file says Zamnagawa, in the 1300s. Then Muhammad Rumfa. The Chronicle says he built a palace and moved in the next year. The year after, he pushed the walls outward, gate by gate. He founded a market, Kurmi, which still trades today. A scholar, al-Maghili, wrote Rumfa a book on how a king should rule. A walled city needs more than walls. Who lived inside them?
scenes.disputed: Who finished Kano's first wall? The Kano Chronicle credits Yusa (1136–1194 by its reckoning); Nigeria's 2007 UNESCO tentative-list file credits Zamnagawa, in the mid-14th century. The age of the Dala settlement also differs: the 7th century (Iliffe) or the 10th (UNESCO file).

scenes.title: Who lived inside the walls

when.label: 1438–1526 · Kano Chronicle reckoning and Leo Africanus

scenes.text: Go back before Rumfa, to King Abdullahi Burja. People already lived inside the first wall. The Chronicle says Burja opened roads from Bornu, in the east, to Gwanja, in the south-west. He was the first in Hausaland to own camels. He was also the first to send tribute to Bornu. His men raided the south for captives, and settled them in twenty-one new towns. Under Yakubu, Fulani came from Mali with books on divinity and etymology. Salt became common in Hausaland. Then came Rumfa: his palace, new walls through named gates, and Kurmi market. Traders and scholars came to the city. Rumfa gave offices of state to eunuchs, and began a council of nine, the Tara-ta-Kano. He began kulle, the seclusion of women, and was the first to have kakaki, long royal trumpets. In his time came Kano's first war with Katsina. It lasted eleven years, and neither side won. Writing in 1526, Leo Africanus described Kano's people as wealthy merchants and skilled craftsmen. Whether he ever went there is doubted. By then, Wangara merchants had probably brought kola nuts into the trade.
scenes.disputed: Did Leo Africanus see Kano? Fisher (1978) doubts that he visited Hausaland at all, so his description is given as his account, not as an eyewitness record. Yakubu's reign is 1452–1463 by the Chronicle's eleven years; one summary starts it in 1432.
